The geometry is a canonical triangle field whose triangles follow typed screw joints, discovered from the video without any joint initialization. The language field is supervised by a t-tagged caption bank that describes each part with comparative state phrases in a whitened open-vocabulary text space. A free-form query is answered by maximizing part relevance jointly over parts and states, which returns both the part and the articulation state it describes; a command is then executed by moving only that part along its recovered joint. On the 100 objects of Articulate-100, ArtLang-4D recovers more accurate joints and part geometry than reconstruction and articulation baselines, retrieves the queried state far more reliably than a state-agnostic language field, and executes language commands with lower motion error.

papers.title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the ROM
papers.summary: Nearly five decades after their introduction, Merkle trees remain the most efficient hash-based vector commitments. They compress a vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ into a commitment whose size is independent of $n$, such that a verifier can open any bit $x_i$ using $\log n$ hash evaluations. The security of the scheme (intractability of finding two distinct openings for a given bit using the same commitment) follows from the collision resistance of the hash function. The verifier's runtime complexity is a bottleneck in many key applications of vector commitments, including SNARKs, credentials, and authenticated dictionaries. As such, a longstanding open question has been whether it is possible to construct hash-based vector commitments where the verifier makes a sublogarithmic number of hash evaluations. We prove that sublogarithmic verifier complexity is impossible to achieve through black-box use of a hash function; we not only rule out constructions from collision resistant hash functions, but in fact show that commitment schemes with sublogarithmic verifier complexity are unachievable in the random oracle model. In particular, any vector commitment with deterministic verifiers has verifier query complexity $Ω_θ(\log n)$, where $θ$ is the input length of the random oracle. This bound is matched up to constant factors by high-arity Merkle trees. The key technical lemma in our proof is a disjoint product lemma, which can be viewed as a computational analog of the van den Berg-Kesten-Reimer (BKR) inequality. We believe this lemma is of independent interest, and in particular may be useful for showing other lower bounds and separations in the random oracle model.

papers.title: A 3D Simulator for Passive SPAD Imaging
papers.summary: Passive single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) cameras provide short-exposure observations for low-light perception, but collecting task annotations for these sensors remains difficult, and annotated datasets are scarce. We present a 3D simulation pipeline that generates realistic photon detections together with camera-motion and semantic labels, enabling perception models to be trained on synthetic SPAD observations and applied directly to real-world data. The pipeline couples controllable scene geometry and motion with a sensor-informed observation model that accounts for photon shot noise, dark counts, and spatial crosstalk. We evaluate the pipeline through calibrated photon-count comparisons and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across three downstream perception tasks. We show that classifiers trained only on synthetic SPAD data achieve high accuracy on real low-light recordings at illumination levels less than 2 lux, without real-data fine-tuning. Similarly, we apply models trained entirely on simulated camera sweeps to real-world camera-rotation estimation and achieve mean absolute rotation errors of less than 1 degree on real 20-degree and 30-degree sweeps at 0.5 and 5.0 lux, when deployed zero-shot. We additionally train semantic segmentation models on synthetic data with automatically generated dense labels and perform direct inference on real-world low-light recordings; the results further demonstrate the usefulness of synthetic dense supervision for real low-light perception. Our simulator thus provides a practical source of annotated training data for real SPAD perception.

papers.title: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.

papers.title: Joint Estimation of Abilities and Item Parameters for Large Language Models Using Probability and Binary Responses: A Fractional-Response IRT Framework
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) evaluations provide two response types: probabilities assigned to correct answers and binary indicators of correctness. Restricting evaluation to one type narrows the range of available models or discards probability information. We propose a method to integrate both types through a common two-parameter logistic item response model and fractional-response quasi-maximum likelihood estimation. The framework includes binary-only models in common-scale evaluation without discarding available probabilityinformation; broader measurement coverage does not by itself ensure greater precision or measurement equivalence. Simulations evaluate statistical efficiency when both response types have the same expected value. Moreover, adding probability respondents improves item calibration more efficiently than adding binary respondents. However, adding noisier binary responses to an already precise probability sample can increase estimation error under equal observation weights. An application to Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) combines probability response data from the Open LLM Leaderboard with binary response data from Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) and reveals model-family response patterns, differences in item characteristics, and systematic ability shifts between evaluation protocols. The proposed framework extends common-scale IRT evaluation to models with different response formats while highlighting the roles of observation variability and evaluation-protocol comparability in statistical efficiency and interpretation.

papers.title: Quantum Noise-Limited Terahertz Interferometry for Distinguishing Ultra-Compact Supermassive Galactic Objects
papers.summary: The images of the galactic centers, M87$^*$ and Sgr~A$^*$, obtained by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) provide hitherto unknown revelations on these supermassive objects. The key issue here is the presence or otherwise of an event horizon at these ultra-compact entities. We show here that distinguishing the central images generated by gravitational lensing of a Schwarzschild black hole and a Joshi--Malafarina--Narayan (JMN-1) central naked singularity provides important insights into the nature of these supermassive objects and would help test the cosmic censorship conjecture, central to black hole physics. For optically thin spherical accretion onto Sgr~A$^*$, their interferometric visibilities become separable, independently of the emission model, on three baseline ranges within 1.4--6.2 G$λ$ at errors of $\simeq36\,μ$Jy, and at $L_\star=2.64\,$G$λ$ at $\simeq71\,μ$Jy. This is about 28 times below the 2017 Event Horizon Telescope statistical uncertainty. We suggest that the widest detection window demands minutes-long coherent integrations, favoring a near-quantum-limited space interferometer.

papers.title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Vulnerability Discovery in Windows Kernel Binaries
papers.summary: Frontier models are increasingly used to discover real-world security vulnerabilities, making it critical to systematically evaluate their cybersecurity capabilities. However, existing security benchmarks primarily focus on known vulnerabilities in open-source projects, largely overlooking closed-source binaries, which underpin much of the software industry. In this paper, we ask: how effective are frontier models at uncovering deep vulnerabilities in production binaries? To answer this question, we present DeepBinary, the first comprehensive benchmark for open-ended vulnerability discovery in Windows kernel binaries. Given a target binary, an agent analyzes it using a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated VMs and reports each vulnerability with a crashing proof of concept (PoC). Unlike existing benchmarks, DeepBinary replays every report on fresh VMs and employs an LLM-based judge to assess its validity, uniqueness, and impact (estimated by bug bounty values). Beyond known vulnerabilities, DeepBinary also enables the discovery and validation of previously unknown (0-day) vulnerabilities. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of representative open- and closed-weight models (including GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) across diverse coding agents (including Codex and Claude Code) on 12 target binaries. In total, they discover over 200 vulnerabilities with an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, including 146 distinct previously unknown vulnerabilities across all experiments. Our results further reveal substantial differences in models' ability to analyze binaries, conduct experiments, and sustain vulnerability discovery over long horizons. Overall, DeepBinary makes long-horizon, open-ended vulnerability discovery in complex binaries measurable, revealing fundamental differences in how frontier models analyze and explore such systems.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks for quark Dyson--Schwinger equations and propagator singularities
papers.summary: We develop a physics-informed neural-network (PINN) framework for solving the rainbow-truncated quark Dyson--Schwinger equation at real and complex momenta. The resulting dressing functions agree closely with conventional iterative solutions. We investigate the singularity structure of the quark propagator using two complementary methods. Analytic continuation of a PINN trained on the real momentum axis estimates the locations of poles and further reveals three complex-conjugate pole pairs. An independent reconstruction using PINN-parametrized spectral densities and a single pole pair yields $q=-0.146\pm0.391i~\mathrm{GeV}^2$. The agreement between the two methods substantially strengthens confidence in the properties of the leading singularities. Both spectral densities change sign, and the negative regions of the vector density and the complex poles indicate a violation of reflection positivity, consistent with quark confinement. Finally, we use the extracted poles and residues to calculate their contributions to two order parameters at finite quark chemical potential, the chiral condensate and the quark number density.

papers.title: DevEx is for Humans, AX is for Agents: Measuring Context Health in Agentic Software Work
papers.summary: Coding agents succeed or fail in the context humans give them, yet most evaluations measure only output. Drawing on developer experience research, we introduce Agent Experience (AX), an instrument that scores session transcripts on four dimensions of the CAFE(S) framework: Clarity, Actionability, Fidelity, and Efficiency; Security, a gate rather than a friction dimension, is out of scope. A rubric-guided language model rates each dimension from 1 to 5 and explains what the human could have provided. We report on three studies that tested this model. In the Stack Overflow Developer Survey, respondents reporting context problems were less likely to rate AI as very useful in all seven activities examined (12-28%). Across 882 rated agentic sessions from a pilot sample of 1,000, Actionability received the lowest ratings (59.6% of ratings at or below 3, versus 26.6% for Fidelity), and ratings were lower in longer sessions. One researcher's unblinded review of 15 randomly sampled sessions found all scores reasonable and explanations supported. In a controlled scenario, we injected context defects into one data-analysis task and ran it twelve times. Every defect condition used more tokens than the clean baseline (mean +91%), and five evaluator models flagged 50-85% of targeted dimensions and 14-36% of non-targeted dimensions. Fidelity defects were detected most consistently and Actionability defects least. Because interventions were imperfectly isolated, these results are exploratory. AX gives teams structured, actionable evidence about context-related friction that complements output and outcome measures.

papers.title: Dynamic Reasoning in Next-Gen Detection and Response: An Empirical Study of LLM Triage, Reinforcement Tuning, and Adversarial Evasion
papers.summary: We present an end-to-end empirical study of dynamic reasoning in next-generation detection and response pipelines, evaluating how static classifiers, graph-based signal fusion, and large language model (LLM) triage agents perform under strict human-analyst attention budgets (Recall at B alerts/day). Across 56 reproducible experiments spanning a multi-layer enterprise-and-cloud simulator and four public datasets (SOREL-20M, BODMAS, LANL, and DARPA Transparent Computing), we test twelve architectural claims governing modern fleet-scale defense. First, we show that fleet growth halves recall at a fixed analyst budget even at negligible compute cost (<$0.0003 per million events), and that rarity-weighted graph risk propagation outperforms GraphSAGE without neural training. Second, evaluating frontier reasoning models (Gemini) and fine-tuned open-weight models (Qwen3-4B) for alert triage reveals that unconstrained LLM auto-closure eliminates 90% of false positives while silently discarding 31-44% of true attack cases. Third, post-training with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) causes severe reward hacking on unseen attack classes, suppressing up to 86% of novel attacks compared to two-epoch supervised fine-tuning. Finally, against an adaptive adversary generating plausible cover stories in benign telemetry fields, LLM triage evasion rises sharply unless gated by a deterministic policy harness prior to model invocation.
papers.comment: 13 pages (main text), 44 pages total with appendices, 5 figures, 56 experiments. Companion architectural design and threat model: https://jeremycanale.com/google-nextgen-detection/

papers.title: SplatWAM: Splatting World Action Models for Real-Time 3D Imagination
papers.summary: World models typically predict future observations in pixel or latent space, limiting their ability to directly represent true 3D scene evolution. We present SplatWAM (Splatting World Action Model), a generative world model that learns action-conditioned dynamics directly over compact 3D Gaussian primitives. A tokenizer SplatWAM-T first encodes a variable number of unposed views into a fixed budget of Gaussian tokens. A dynamics model SplatWAM-D then predicts future Gaussian states in a single forward pass per action, using log-Euclidean covariance coordinates and differentiable rendering supervision to facilitate learning in an explicit 3D space. Each predicted state can be rasterized from arbitrary viewpoints, enforcing a shared 3D representation across views by construction. On OGBench Scene, SplatWAM renders novel views 12x faster than video world models (~80 FPS on an RTX 5090) with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR. We further introduce SplatWAM-P, a lightweight flow-matching policy head jointly trained with the dynamics model. Across 8 task suites, model-free Gaussian-token policies outperform pixel-based counterparts by up to 24.8 percentage points. SplatWAM-P improves over Latent Particle World Model (LPWM) by 12 percentage points and matches HIQL without a learned value function. On LIBERO, our ~1B model outperforms WorldVLA (~7B) and the robot-pretrained OpenVLA (~7B), while matching OpenVLA-OFT when both are trained without large-scale robot pretraining. Code and checkpoints will be released.

papers.title: Fast Muscle-Driven Whole-Body Motion Tracking with a Differentiable World Model
papers.summary: Tracking motion capture with a whole-body musculoskeletal model means coordinating hundreds of muscles through contact, and current controllers take hours to days of GPU time to train, so every tuning decision is expensive. SuperMimic trains a tracking policy by backpropagating through the rollouts of a learned world model. We extend it to MS-Human-700 (700 muscles) and MyoFullBody (354 muscles), with MuJoCo's activation dynamics inside the world model. To make its training fast, our recipe takes the speedups developed for the Unitree G1, replaces three of their settings that fail on muscles, and adds four changes of our own: observations without muscle geometry, data collection concurrent with the updates, Beta exploration noise that keeps every excitation in $[0,1]$, and 50 Hz control. On one RTX 5090 it trains MS-Human-700 in 6.3 minutes to the held-out return that SuperMimic's published hyperparameters reach in 3.9 hours, 37$\times$ sooner, and in 20 minutes to lower tracking errors than theirs after 10 hours. It trains MyoFullBody 34$\times$ sooner without retuning. Ablations show what is specific to muscles: a higher policy learning rate stalls half of the runs, and clipped Gaussian noise adds a tonic co-contraction that Beta noise avoids. Finally, refining the policy's actions through the world model at test time lowers the position error by a further 26% with no held-out clip failing, and reaches the same return after 5.1 instead of 6.3 minutes of training. Code, the training recipe and videos are on the project page https://muscle-supermimic.beanpow.top.

papers.title: The Information Content of News Embeddings
papers.summary: Does the predictive success of news embeddings reflect a better measure of news surprises or other sources of return predictability in text? We decompose news embeddings by content into event-category, firm-identity, and idiosyncratic components, and by timing into historical levels and current deviations. At short horizons, event categories account for most of the predictive power of embedding forecasts, and simple forecasts based on historical average returns after news in each event category outperform them. At longer horizons, firm information already present in earlier news coverage accounts for a substantial share of return predictability, even after residualization on firm characteristics. The dominance of event categories persists, and historical levels still contribute in the first months, when using a language model pretrained entirely before our sample period. For Llama-2, even embeddings constructed from news more than three years old predict returns at long horizons. However, its predictive advantage over RoBERTa is concentrated in firm identity and the historical level, and its advantage in these components largely disappears by its pretraining cutoff. A calibration shows that pretraining memory, a source of look-ahead bias, can account for this pattern. Describing news more fully is not the same as measuring news surprises, and persistent return predictability from news text does not by itself establish slow incorporation of news into prices.

papers.title: SecID: An LLM-Guided Framework for Threat-Aware Secondary Asset Identification with Quantitative RTL Analysis
papers.summary: The growing complexity of modern hardware designs is making security assurance increasingly difficult. One of the foundational steps in pre-silicon security verification is identifying security assets. While primary assets are often evident from design functionality, the internal signals that can facilitate their compromise are much less apparent. Complex data- and control-flow dependencies create many such internal security-critical locations, whose exploitation depends on the threat-specific attack mechanism---these are the secondary assets. To precisely identify these, we propose SecID, a multi-agent framework that combines deterministic RTL analysis with bounded dynamic evaluation and LLM reasoning to identify threat-specific secondary assets. Each asset decision is supported by functional influence, threat features, and explicit attack mechanisms. We demonstrate SecID on seven open-source SoC and IP designs, including openMSP430, NEORV32, and CV32E40P. The experimental results are corroborated through comparison with prior work, fault simulation, and formal analysis, and further evaluated through pipeline- and final-stage ablation, threshold-sensitivity studies, and final-stage repeatability analysis. Together, these evaluations show that SecID can identify highly threat-relevant secondary assets with respect to a given primary asset, providing a scalable path toward hardware-security verification.
papers.comment: This paper will be presented at Design, Automation and Test in Europe Conference (DATE) 2027

papers.title: Functional Direct Binomial Regression for Right-Censored Competing Risks Data
papers.summary: Existing regression-based methods for functional predictors often overlook right-censored competing risks outcomes, limiting their applicability in many biomedical studies. To address this gap, this article proposes a functional direct binomial model for right-censored competing risks data, where a binary outcome indicates the occurrence of an event of interest before a fixed time horizon. The model enables straightforward prediction of the cumulative incidence function, can be fitted using standard, scalable algorithms for large-scale studies, and has broad applications to functional predictors, such as wearable device data. We establish large-sample theory to facilitate inference, including hypothesis testing and the construction of confidence intervals and bands for both scalar coefficients and functional parameters. The methodology is further extended to accommodate multiple functional biomarkers and to handle missing failure causes. Simulation studies confirm that the proposed method provides accurate estimation and valid inference. We illustrate the approach with an application to modeling time to advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) in the presence of the competing risk of death, leveraging continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data and baseline covariates. The analysis shows that CGM is both a significant predictor and a viable alternative to the traditional HbA1c biomarker for CKD.

papers.title: APEX: Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration
papers.summary: Ensemble-based methods provide a practical framework for history matching, prediction, and optimization of subsurface models. In methodological studies, however, performance is rarely assessed from a single run. Comparisons typically span cases, configurations, and random seeds, while each evaluation may require an expensive external simulator. Keeping such studies computationally bounded, auditable, and reproducible therefore requires more than implementing a numerical method: experiments must be validated before execution, computational costs estimated, repeated runs organized consistently, and configurations and outputs made traceable. To address these needs, we developed APEX (Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration), an open-source Python platform that provides a common framework for configuring, validating, executing, recording, and comparing ensemble-based experiments. APEX is organized around three concepts: an experiment defines what is executed, a run records a single execution, and a study coordinates and compares multiple experiments or runs. Experiments are specified through validated configurations, which can also be generated by a planner agent. Before execution, APEX estimates the maximum number of forward simulations required. If the estimate exceeds a user-defined threshold, submission is held for approval. Each run records provenance information, while studies repeat problems across variants and paired replicates and compare results using paired statistical analyses. Scientific and computational components, including methods, simulators, metrics, and optimizers, are implemented as plugins. A command line interface, Python client, REST service with a web interface, and tools for language model agents access these capabilities through a common service layer.

papers.title: Adaptive confidence bands for a continuous treatment effect curve under shape constraints
papers.summary: In causal inference with observational data new inferential targets arise when treatment is continuous rather than discrete. Here we form (simultaneous) confidence bands over the continuous treatment effect curve. We form confidence bands based on assuming the curve satisfies shape constraints of either monotonicity or concavity, under the assumption of no unmeasured confounding. As is commonly the case, two nuisance functions arise, and our bands are asymptotically valid if the product of the error rates of the two nuisance functions is small enough. We also develop non-causal shape constrained bands in regression with fixed or random non-uniform grid which are of independent interest. Furthermore, our bands are adaptive to a range of function flatness and smoothness levels in that when the true flatness/smoothness level is unknown the bands still achieve the same (optimal) rate of convergence (in sup-norm) as when the true smoothness level is known. We demonstrate these bands through simulations and an application to the effect of nurse staffing on hospital performance.

papers.title: OnCue: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios under Occlusion with Temporal Control
papers.summary: Occluded hazards challenge autonomous driving because visibility timing determines available avoidance actions. Existing scenario generators control hazard motion without jointly specifying exposure and reference-contact times. We propose OnCue, a framework that generates safety-critical encounters in real driving logs with these temporal conditions. Scene geometry provides hidden starts and timed waypoints for pedestrian, cyclist, and vehicle trajectory generation. An offline response oracle labels encounters as Reactive (avoidable after exposure) or Anticipatory (avoidable only with earlier visibility) and stores safe maneuvers as training demonstrations. On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, 90.1-96.6% of valid trajectories meet both requested times within +/-0.2 s. OnCue matches the requested reaction window between them in 92.8% of shared vehicle requests versus at most 42.1% for adapted adversarial generators. Across matched cyclist encounters, longer windows lower PDM-Closed collision from 59.1% to 5.5%, while the learned planner LatentDriver shows the opposite trend. OnCue demonstrations reduce LatentDriver target collision by 54.8 points on held-out Reactive tests, but reduce overall no-target progress by 12.7 m. These results highlight the value of temporal control for evaluating and improving planners under occlusion.

papers.title: Low-latency gravitational wave alert infrastructure and new data products for multi-messenger astronomy during LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA's fourth observing run
papers.summary: Multi-messenger investigations of compact object mergers, such as binary neutron star and neutron star-black hole systems, remain among the most dynamic frontiers of modern astronomy. During the fourth observing run of Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, and KAGRA, the search for joint electromagnetic and neutrino counterparts to gravitational-wave signals continued using public, semi-automated data products distributed in near real-time. The sky localizations and preliminary source characterizations provided by these alerts helped guide multiple rapid follow-up observations to candidate gravitational-wave events. During this run, the low-latency search parameter space was expanded to include the sub-solar mass regime and associated public data products were developed. Further, chirp mass estimates of the binary merger system were introduced as a new public data product and distributed to enable follow-up searches to concentrate their resources on the most promising transients. In order to streamline the implementation of new searches and data products, a mock data challenge, known as the Low-Latency Production Integration Challenge (LLPIC), was used as a replay of a simulated population of gravitational-wave sources to optimize and profile the software infrastructure and scientific deliverables. In this paper we describe these new public data products, their performance and the result of end-to-end testing of the low-latency infrastructure with the LLPIC.

papers.title: An Adversarial Multi-Agent Pursuit Game for Locomotor Agility Pretraining
papers.summary: Agile humanoid locomotion requires controllers that can adapt to rapidly changing motion demands while remaining stable and robust. Recent locomotion controllers are typically designed with either a dense reward that is carefully shaped to encourage steps and penalize falling, or by using a reference tracking reward which teaches the controller to follow predetermined motions. Once a behavior that maximizes the reward is discovered, the controller ceases to learn. While generally stable, reference tracking methods focus on motor control separately from motion generation. Self-play has been proven as an effective technique for superhuman performance on several multiagent games like Go, Starcraft, hide-and-seek, and capture-the-flag. We train neural networks to play the game of multiagent tag in a physics simulator to study if new motion generation and control strategies can emerge through sparse feedback and competitive self-play. We present MJTag, a task suite for role-conditioned locomotion during competitive pursuit-evasion. Our model is a role-conditioned policy for a low-level locomotion controller and optional planar velocity commands. MJTag's league-based play with sparse feedback enables a locomotion controller to adopt new strategies, including dodging, sprinting, and tackling.

papers.title: WADJET: Whole-Job Authorization and Dispatch for Job Execution Trust on FPGA System-on-Chip Accelerators
papers.summary: On an FPGA system-on-chip, the software that submits work to an accelerator also decides what the accelerator does. It writes the registers one by one, and the hardware runs whatever it finds, so faulty or compromised software can change one address or resend a job. Existing protections decide who may reach an accelerator or keep its data safe. Deciding whether one job was approved and is still unused takes three things in one place: the only way to the accelerator, the whole job held back until checked, and a record of used approvals. WADJET puts the three in one gate in FPGA logic. A separate authority encrypts and authenticates each approved job, with a sequence number, using Ascon-AEAD128. The gate verifies the whole job before releasing any part, accepts only a newer sequence number, uses it up, and writes the registers of an unmodified accelerator itself. The gate replaces only the processor's direct line to the registers and works beside the existing protections. In a software model, a check on each write ran jobs mixed from two approved ones; the whole-job rule released none. Its release path is proven on the Verilog for all inputs. On a Zynq-7020 running a language model, it released all 21,000 approved jobs and none of 14,700 altered or repeated ones. It needs a third of the lookup tables of ShEF's register protection, which protects more, and adds about ten microseconds to starting a job. It assumes trusted control of its key, reset, and configuration.
papers.comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to Microprocessors and Microsystems

papers.title: Best-of-$N$ Test-Time Steering Can Lead to Reward Hacking in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but adapting to changing environmental conditions still remains challenging. Recent test-time steering methods have shown promise in enabling adaptive VLA policies by utilizing additional computation during deployment. In this paper, we consider best-of-$N$ test-time steering for VLA models, where multiple action candidates are sampled from a fixed policy and a verifier is used to select the best one during deployment. We show that increasing $N$ does not always improve performance when the verifier is inaccurate, and can favor candidates whose scores exploit prediction errors, a form of reward hacking. We study this effect on 60 LIBERO-Safety task-level cases using a $π_{0.5}$ policy, with ten repetitions per case. We introduce controlled errors in a MuJoCo trajectory verifier and show that as $N$ increases, selected candidate rewards diverge from the accurate verifier rewards, leading to reward hacking. We also show that verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection can mitigate reward hacking in some settings.
papers.comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, to be presented at 1st Workshop on Physical World AI at NeurIPS 2026

papers.title: RoboARC: Physical Puzzles for Robotic Manipulation under Spatial Constraints
papers.summary: Many hard manipulation tasks come down to a spatial constraint that only a few motions satisfy, such as passing a part through a gap barely wider than itself or separating two interlocked parts. These motions depend on the exact geometry of each scene, so demonstrations and skills recorded elsewhere rarely transfer. We therefore ask: when manipulation hinges on spatial constraints, can robots reason out the right motions? We introduce RoboARC, a benchmark of 90 tasks in six constraint types over rigid and soft materials, on three robots in MuJoCo. Every task is a frozen scene with a physics-based grader and a verified reference solution that replays bit-identically. Each task comes in a Privileged regime, with the full simulator state and resets, and a Standard regime with real-sensor inputs (camera images and proprioception) and a single attempt without resets. We evaluate seven coding agents and four VLA policies, none trained on these tasks. The strongest agent, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, solves 86% of the tasks in the Privileged regime and 43% in the Standard regime, and the four VLA policies, run zero-shot, solve none of their 18 one-arm puzzles. On 15 puzzles that GPT-6 Astra solved in the Privileged regime and failed in the Standard regime, object poses add 4 points and part geometry 13, but both together add 36, from 24% to 60%. Only 7% of the coding agents' failed runs pass more than half of a task, and 53% of the failed runs in the Standard regime are stuck on a single step. Frontier coding agents already reason out the right motions for many of these tasks once they know where the parts are and what shape they have. From their own sensors, in a single attempt, the strongest solves fewer than half of the tasks. The website can be found at https://roboarc.embodied-first-exam.ai

papers.title: Poisoning Self-Evolving Security Policies in LLM Agents
papers.summary: Self-evolving defenses improve LLM-agent security by learning reusable policies from observed attacks. However, we demonstrate that this learning process itself can become an attack surface. Using SED (Self-Evolving Defense) in the AgentDojo benchmark, we construct a single prompt-injection episode that causes the defense to learn an over-broad policy and subsequently refuse legitimate requests. Across 10 Nemotron runs, every poisoned run over-refuses at least one legitimate task, while unrelated-task performance remains unchanged and the original prompt-injection defense remains effective. The attack also transfers to gpt-oss-120b; however, its poisoning mechanism depends on a successful initial prompt injection and therefore fails to activate when the target agent resists the underlying injection. In contrast, integrity-oriented attacks targeting SED's judge, policy synthesis, retrieval, and organization mechanisms fail in our evaluated settings, identifying over-refusal as the primary exploitable failure mode observed in our experiments. We further identify self-poisoning from false-positive harm judgments without an attacker. Finally, contrastive policy synthesis and an automatic broadness-check gate substantially reduce, but do not eliminate over-refusal, without compromising security in our evaluated settings.

papers.title: Modular fluctuation relations on local causal horizons
papers.summary: Local causal horizons provide a setting for studying horizon thermodynamics in the neighborhood of any regular spacetime point. Here, we investigate this description beyond mean energy and entropy balances by studying fluctuations of boost-energy transfer induced by unitary perturbations of the horizon reference state. Using the modular structure of the horizon algebra and a thermal reference state, we construct an energy transfer probability measure and derive integral and detailed fluctuation relations with the mean entropy production being expressed in terms of the Araki relative entropy. The formulation accommodates type-III algebras without introducing a reduced density matrix and can be extended to global bifurcate Killing horizons admitting the required thermal reference state. For coherent scalar-field perturbations, we obtain a closed form for the characteristic function, identify the mean transfer with the excess boost-energy flux, and derive a thermodynamic uncertainty relation bounding the variance in terms of the mean transfer. We then explore the geometric implications by postulating a stochastic horizon entropy--area correspondence that associates an area change with each counted energy transfer. Under this additional hypothesis, we obtain fluctuation relations for area changes and an area change uncertainty bound for coherent perturbations.

papers.title: FOCI: Trajectory Optimization on Gaussian Splats for Gaussian Robots
papers.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently gained popularity as a faster alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) in 3D reconstruction and view synthesis methods. Leveraging the spatial information encoded in 3DGS, this work proposes FOCI (Field Overlap Collision Integral), an algorithm that is able to optimize trajectories directly on the Gaussians themselves. FOCI leverages a novel and interpretable collision formulation for 3DGS using the notion of the overlap integral between Gaussians. The formulation presented applies to different robot morphologies (e.g., fixed and mobile base manipulators, legged robots, UAVs) and handles both static and dynamic Gaussian-Splat environments. Contrary to other approaches, which represent the robot with conservative bounding boxes that underestimate the traversability of the environment, we propose to represent the environment and the robot as Gaussian Splats. This not only has desirable computational properties, but also allows for orientation-aware planning, allowing the robot to pass through very tight and narrow spaces. We extensively test our algorithm in both synthetic and real Gaussian Splats, showcasing that collision-free trajectories for legged, aerial and manipulator robots can be computed in seconds, even with hundreds of thousands of Gaussians making up the environment. The code is available at https://github.com/leggedrobotics/foci

papers.title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Total Kinetic Energy Distributions in Neutron-Induced Fission
papers.summary: The incident-neutron-energy dependence of post-neutron total-kinetic-energy (TKE) distributions, particularly their width in the multichance-fission regime, provides a sensitive test of fission calculations. We investigate how the General Description of Fission Observables (GEF) and probabilistic machine-learning models trained on GEF reproduce measured TKE distributions, emphasizing their width at high incident-neutron energies and extrapolation beyond the training range. Gaussian process regression (GPR), GPR with a white-noise kernel, a mixture density network (MDN), and a Bayesian mixture density network (BMDN) are evaluated on a common calculated dataset. An extended MDN/BMDN analysis uses 1,025 GEF spectra from 20 target nuclei and 60 measured distributions. Training ranges of up to 20, 40, and approximately 76 MeV are compared with matched-size controls extending to 30 or 40 MeV while preserving the number of spectra per target. Above 40 MeV, the BMDN width mean absolute error relative to experiment decreases from 5.63 MeV for training up to 20 MeV to 2.70 and 2.53 MeV for two matched-size 30-MeV controls and 1.77 MeV for the matched-size 40-MeV control. Predictive-interval coverage relative to GEF above 40 MeV rises from 52.3% to 92.3% between the 20-MeV and full training ranges. Agreement with measured mean TKE and widths is target dependent, with no uniform ordering among GEF, MDN, and BMDN. The results demonstrate the sensitivity of high-energy widths to training-energy coverage, with improvements already evident at 30 MeV. The comparatively slow variation of GEF widths at high energies limits the extent to which these improvements can be attributed to learning nontrivial energy dependence. Adequate training-energy coverage is critical for reproducing the calculated high-energy evolution, while agreement with experiment remains constrained by the underlying fission model.

papers.title: From Conversations to Commitments: A Design Study of Shared Records for Agent-to-Business Coordination
papers.summary: Business commitments require accepted terms to be linked to delegated authority, reserved resources and durable evidence. We examine how a shared, attributable interaction record can support these links across independently operated organisations. Talea combines signed AT Protocol records with A2A task execution. We use its coordination sandbox and a proposed commercial extension in a design study of an airline booking disrupted passengers into three competing hotels. Four observations follow. First, AT Protocol provides mechanisms supporting five of six coordination requirements, while record-level access and release controls require additional enforcement. Second, the case's confidentiality constraints restrict each hotel's authorised view to its bilateral exchange; only the airline can correlate all three deals. Third, this leaves a possible benefit for late-joining participants inside the airline's trust boundary, but does not establish an advantage over an equally instrumented point-to-point design. Fourth, a deterministic release interface constrains fixed, approved payloads but cannot bound disclosure when negotiated values depend on private state. Finite-model explorations and deterministic interface checks reproduce the specified behaviours and counterexamples when selected controls are removed. They do not measure comparative benefit or validate a deployed commercial system. The remaining hypothesis is that, within one trust boundary, shared records improve decision reconstruction and recovery under changing participation relative to point-to-point exchange with equivalent authority, reservation, retention and correlation evidence. We specify an experiment to test it.

papers.title: RegionAlign: Manipulating Parameter Layouts for Localized Fault Injection on LLMs and VLMs
papers.summary: Physical fault injection can flip stored weight bits, degrading LLMs and VLMs. Existing work largely overlooks how supply-chain manipulation affects fault vulnerability. We introduce RegionAlign, which allows a malicious provider to manipulate only the parameter layout before deployment, using bit-sensitivity search and channel permutations to concentrate vulnerable bits in one memory region while preserving weight values and clean performance. Under matched budgets, software experiments show greater degradation from search-selected in-region flips with RegionAlign than with original or random layouts. EMFI feasibility study confirms weight corruption. RegionAlign reveals a stealthy supply-chain threat that layout manipulation weakens physical fault resilience.

papers.title: Hamiltonian approach to isospectrality in nonrotating black holes
papers.summary: In this work, we revisit the isospectrality of black hole perturbations from a Hamiltonian perspective. For a nonrotating, uncharged system, we present a convenient canonical description of the background degrees of freedom that facilitates comparison with the usual Lagrangian formulation. This allows us to identify phase-space counterparts of the superpotential and the algebraically special modes and show that they satisfy the expected isospectral relations, at least on shell or off shell modulo some subtle lapse redefinitions. Finally, we investigate the extent to which these results persist in theories that effectively modify general relativity. In this setting, we formally quantify the corresponding deviations from the classical relations and the associated potential violations of isospectrality to first order in the modifications.

papers.title: DDxBasis: Explaining Frozen Foundation Encoder-based Medical Classification by Exact Differential Diagnosis
papers.summary: In differential diagnosis (DDx), a clinician explains a diagnosis by the few findings that separate it from the alternatives. Medical image classifiers cannot yet explain themselves this way. Existing explanations are either faithful but spread over hundreds of concepts, or compact but leave part of each decision unexplained. We present DDxBasis, which explains a classifier on a frozen foundation encoder as a differential diagnosis in three steps. First, a concept bottleneck reads all patch tokens at every encoder layer using gated, second-order slot attention. A concept basis then regroups the concepts into two-pole axes, each a differential between groups of diagnoses. Finally, we read a differential diagnosis from each axis through the typical presentation of its poles, the pertinent findings of the case, and counterfactual edits of borderline cases. Across five medical datasets, DDxBasis is the most accurate frozen-encoder model and close to the best published domain-specific results. Because every concept adds its own evidence, its reproducible concept basis splits each decision exactly, at no cost in accuracy. Without ordered stage or concept labels, the axes recover cell lineages and rare subtypes, agree with dermatologists' structure annotations, and expose planted and real shortcuts.

papers.title: The Marauder's Map: Bézier Manifolds Reveal Hidden Surfaces for Model Merging and Ensembling
papers.summary: Neural circuits are famously more robust than deep networks. This is often explained through degeneracy, where structurally distinct configurations support the same function. However, real biological systems exhibit a more flexible form of degeneracy in which specialized circuits continually adapt towards new competencies through localized changes while preserving existing function. Deep learning studies degeneracy through mode connectivity, which connects same-task networks by low-loss curves, sheets, or volumes. However, the field lacks a counterpart to flexible degeneracy, which demands more than ordinary mode connectivity. Defining such an analogue requires asking whether many independently initialized models trained on distinct tasks can be connected by a high-dimensional region of multi-task solutions. We introduce $\textit{Nimbus}$, which learns a high-dimensional Bézier manifold connecting $N$ specialists, going beyond the one-dimensional paths and two-dimensional sheets of mode connectivity work. A naive parameterization would scale combinatorially with $N$, but $\textit{Nimbus}$ requires learning corrections of only 3 interaction orders, showing that the connecting manifold has surprisingly low complexity yet supports multi-task competencies. The resulting manifold forms a navigable "Marauder's Map" that connects specialist models through a shared geometry of competent solutions. Trained across vision and language domains, $\textit{Nimbus}$ produces manifolds that are functionally and locally weight-flat: ensembles sampled from them degrade more gracefully than baselines under input and weight perturbations, with the largest gains in NLL loss and calibration error. $\textit{Nimbus}$ supplies a deep learning interpretation of flexible degeneracy, recasting model connectivity from a low-dimensional path between distant solutions into a high-dimensional volume of nearby ones.

papers.title: Why Does Sensor Depth Fail Learned Manipulation Policies? Finding the Failure Mode with ACT
papers.summary: Learned manipulation policies, from task-specific imitation policies to vision-language-action (VLA) models, rely primarily on RGB images. While some studies report gains from sensor depth, others avoid depth cameras because of measurement noise. Depth cameras introduce both noise and missing depth values (holes), whose relative effects remain unclear. In this study, we calibrate a sensor model using a real wrist-mounted stereo camera and separately evaluate noise and holes on RGB-D imitation policies with three visual encoders in simulation. We found that complete depth improves success by approximately ten percentage points, and most of this gain persists even at twenty times the camera's noise level. In contrast, holes covering about one-sixth of the wrist image eliminate the detectable benefit of depth. The validity mask strongly influences depth reliance: marking a small fraction of pixels as invalid reduces reliance, while filling holes and marking them valid restores most of the benefit. Policies trained on clean depth also lose performance when holes appear only at deployment, sometimes falling below RGB-only performance. These findings suggest that depth cameras for learned policies should therefore be judged by depth coverage more than measurement precision.

papers.title: Geodesic Causal Forests: Learning Heterogeneous Treatment Effects for Random Objects
papers.summary: Causal forests and orthogonal learners estimate heterogeneous treatment effects for scalar or Euclidean outcomes, yet outcomes are increasingly random objects, such as compositions, covariance matrices, distributions, or networks, in metric spaces without linear structure. We introduce geodesic causal forests for conditional geodesic treatment effects. Geodesic transport moves each geodesic between conditional Fréchet means of the potential outcomes to a common reference, making effects comparable across individuals. Because random objects cannot be added or subtracted, Euclidean residual corrections are unavailable; we instead correct the squared-distance loss through which the forest selects splits and estimates effects. The loss is real-valued for every candidate effect, so the correction requires only Fréchet means and leaves second-order nuisance error; for Euclidean outcomes, it recovers doubly robust learning. We establish consistency, convergence rates, and split-selection guarantees under conditions verified for curved and nonsmooth spaces. In simulations with covariance-matrix outcomes, the correction substantially reduces estimation error. For women's livelihood compositions in BRAC's randomized antipoverty program in Bangladesh, new livestock work mainly replaces casual wage work; after alignment, a single effect reproduces much of the variation in percentage-point changes across baseline activities, and the fitted effects are largest among former domestic workers and older women.

papers.title: Escape Time with Quenched Extrinsic Fluctuations in Positive Feedback Systems
papers.summary: Gene regulatory networks with positive feedback often exhibit multiple stable steady states representing distinct cellular phenotypes, allowing stochastic fluctuations to drive phenotypic switching between basins of attraction. Such transitions are commonly characterized by escape-time statistics. While previous studies have typically analyzed intrinsic fluctuation or dynamical environmental fluctuation separately, the combined effect of intrinsic biochemical fluctuation and quenched (slowly varying) extrinsic cell-to-cell parameter heterogeneity on population-level switching dynamics remains less understood. In this study, we formulate a theoretical framework to compute escape-time moments by combining the backward chemical Fokker--Planck equation with population averaging over a stationary distribution of kinetic parameters. We apply this approach to two paradigmatic bistable motifs---positive autoregulation and the genetic Toggle Switch---and quantify how quenched extrinsic heterogeneity modifies switching times across a population of autonomous cells. Our results show that extrinsic parameter variability can substantially alter the mean switching time and, more prominently, increase its dispersion, producing highly heterogeneous switching kinetics across genetically identical cells. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for cell-to-cell parameter heterogeneity when characterizing stochastic phenotypic switching in biological populations.

papers.title: Who Attributes a Mind to Whom? Mutual Theory of Mind in Simulated User-Assistant Conversation
papers.summary: When users assume that an AI chatbot has mental states, they are more likely to develop over-reliance, emotional dependence, and in extreme cases, psychological harm or self-harm. However, how these mind attributions arise in conversations and how human or AI factors influence this is still unknown. We study how users attribute minds using a minimal framework: a simulated user with different characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory. We also introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. Our results show that, on average, nine out of thirteen characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant. We found that relational needs such as attachment anxiety raised it as theory predicts, some general personality traits raised it as well, and AI-specific characteristics the least. By contrast, the assistant's social style barely changed simulated users' mind attribution. Instead, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Memory raised users' attribution only with some user models. The model playing the user changed overall attribution and the effects of characteristics, style, and memory. Our framework measures how persona descriptions affect mind attribution in simulation. It gives concrete hypotheses for human studies and shows the need for more consistent user simulators.

papers.title: Quasinormal modes of black holes in astrophysical environments: Rainbow in the dark matter
papers.summary: Matter around black holes affects the ringdown in two ways: through the background geometry and through the response of the matter itself. We compute axial and polar gravitational quasinormal modes of a black hole embedded in a relativistic Hernquist-type dark matter halo, following the fundamental mode and the first three overtones associated with the vacuum Schwarzschild spectrum. The polar sector couples metric and matter perturbations. At small halo compactness, both sectors follow the familiar gravitational redshift law. Most of the departure from the typical redshift at larger compactness is accounted for by the exact horizon lapse factor of the background. The remaining residual departure to this lapse is sector dependent. Axial and polar frequencies are split, with their splitting growing from the fundamental through the third overtone. At large halo compactness the split grows by an order of magnitude, while overtone-to-fundamental frequency ratios depart from a common rescaling. Within the adopted dark matter profile, the halo acts on the ringdown as a prism that disperses the gravitational spectrum, leaving a parity-dependent imprint that no common rescaling of the frequencies can reproduce. Parity-isospectrality is, thus, broken.

papers.title: Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger: The $Δ(1232)$ Resonance in Supernova QCD Axion Emission
papers.summary: The high-energy tail of supernova axion emission controls searches whose response grows with axion energy. We identify a novel production channel, in which the axion is emitted through an intermediate $Δ(1232)$ resonance, which adds a hard component to the spectrum. We calculate the axion production rate from nucleon-nucleon Bremsstrahlung in chiral effective field theory through next-to-leading order. Including the $Δ(1232)$ roughly doubles the luminosity at one second after bounce and increases the number of escaping axions above $200$ MeV by a factor of about $3$ over the first nine seconds, relative to the nucleon-only calculation. Adding this new production channel roughly doubles $γ$-ray counts from conversion in the progenitor's magnetic field and increases water-Cherenkov counts by about an order of magnitude through its combined effects on emission and absorption. The same hard component can mimic a higher core temperature or thermal-pion emission in $γ$-ray spectral fits. The $Δ(1232)$ resonance is therefore crucial for predicting supernova axion signals and interpreting their spectra.

papers.title: Chaotic singularities inside vacuum black holes
papers.summary: According to the conjecture of Belinski, Khalatnikov and Lifshitz, general relativity gives rise to chaotic dynamics in the vicinity of generic spacelike singularities. However, no vacuum black hole has been shown to exhibit this behaviour. Here we construct stationary, asymptotically locally AdS$_5$ black holes with regular, triaxially squashed horizons and causal exteriors, whose homogeneous interiors realize the cosmological billiard of generic five-dimensional vacuum gravity. We identify a simple algebraic condition on the horizon data that is necessary for the interior billiard to be chaotic, and show that solutions with regular horizons locally access an open set of billiard trajectories.

papers.title: Bounds on Love Numbers and Quasinormal Modes from the Surface Impedance
papers.summary: The surface impedance of a body is fixed by its interior alone and encodes its entire tidal response. We derive bounds on Love numbers and quasinormal modes from constraints on the impedance that follow from either of two properties of a stable body: it is lossless, meaning that it dissipates no energy, or it is passive, meaning that it never gives back more energy than it has received. For a lossless body, every dynamical Love number is bounded from above and below, exactly in general relativity, in any renormalization scheme and at any scale. Earlier bounds are exact for Newtonian stars but fail for compact stars, because they take the response to arbitrarily fast tides to be zero or non-negative, whereas in general relativity it is negative. The quasinormal modes of a lossless body are also excluded from a region of the complex frequency plane set by the mass and radius. Each known Love number enlarges the excluded region. Conversely, the quasinormal modes bound each Love number from below, given the lower ones. For a passive body of horizon scale, such as a black hole, the static Love number lies in a window that closes onto the vanishing black-hole value as the body's surface approaches the horizon.

papers.title: Unitarization from Spin Geometry
papers.summary: We derive the dimensional reduction of 10D super Yang-Mills theory on a general closed 6D spin manifold using spectral decompositions for the higher-dimensional gauge field and gaugino, keeping the infinite towers of Kaluza-Klein (KK) modes in the lower-dimensional theory. We then calculate tree-level $2 \rightarrow 2$ scattering amplitudes with external massive spinors and vectors in this lower-dimensional theory. By studying the high-energy behavior of these amplitudes and imposing perturbative unitarity, we derive several sum rules that involve the eigenvalues of Laplace and Dirac operators on the internal 6-manifold, together with products of cubic coupling constants of the KK modes. These give concrete realizations of the known unitarity sum rules for spontaneously broken gauge theories. We illustrate explicitly how the simplest sum rule is satisfied for flat tori and round spheres.

papers.title: The black hole IR triangle for scalar QED
papers.summary: We construct the black hole infrared triangle of scalar QED on a stretched Schwarzschild horizon at tree level. In the covariant phase space of the near-horizon Maxwell field, the soft charge is a corner term. The memory is the zero mode of the gauge-invariant radiative field along the generators. It is conjugate to the boundary gauge mode that labels the degenerate horizon vacua, and Gauss' law fixes it by the flux of charge through the horizon. The Noether flux of the residual gauge transformation through the stretched horizon is not conserved by the scattering, because charged matter crosses the stretched horizon in both directions. The flux with its matter part removed is the soft charge, which generates the large gauge transformation. Its Ward identity is equivalent to a soft photon theorem in every radiative partial wave, which we derive from the near-horizon Feynman rules and, where these do not control the emission, from the field equations at leading order. The main difference from null infinity is that on a stretched horizon both radial branches of the field are independent boundary data. The hard charge is a radial flux. With both branches present it weights each leg by the direction of its radial motion, and the soft factor is a sign per leg. The endpoint data on the two branches give two boundary observables, the time-integrated transverse magnetic and electric fields. The field radiated by a scattering process contributes only to the first, where it cancels the change in the Coulomb memory of the charges, so that the soft charge is conserved. A charge that crosses the horizon enters both. We also discuss the infrared divergence, the dressing of the external states, and the fate of the memory in the Hartle--Hawking state, where it performs a random walk driven by the Hawking radiation.

papers.title: Resolving the Conformal Mode Problem with Einstein-Cartan Gravity
papers.summary: We show that, when $Λ> 0$, the conformal factor problem is absent in first order Einstein-Cartan gravity in which the spin connection and tetrad are independent off-shell. At fixed connection, a conformal rescaling of the tetrad produces no conformal kinetic term so that the action is bounded from below. The original unbounded Einstein-Hilbert action, the Einstein-Hilbert action without the problematic conformal kinetic term and conformally invariant $R^{2}/Λ$ gravity arise as classical saddles of the Einstein-Cartan action with respect to the connection and conformal mode of the tetrad.

papers.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
papers.summary: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/

papers.title: The double copy and perturbative teleparallel gravity
papers.summary: In this paper we analyze the double copy between gluon and graviton amplitudes within the context of teleparallel gravity. We first set up an effective Lagrangian based on minimal assumptions which reproduces the on-shell amplitudes stemming from the double-copy procedure. By straightforwardly computing the three- and four-point amplitude, this double-copy Lagrangian can be constrained up to a few real parameters when expanding to quartic order. For a specific choice of parameters, we find an exact equivalence with perturbative teleparallel gravity. This suggests that the teleparallel formulation might be well suited to make the double copy more transparent from a Lagrangian viewpoint.

papers.title: PyRUA-Dex: Learning Programmatic Policies for Dexterous Bimanual Manipulation with Coding Agents
papers.summary: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.
papers.comment: 23 pages, 9 figures, 7 tables. Project page: https://vme0522.github.io/PyRUA-Dex/

papers.title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification
papers.summary: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.

papers.title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
papers.summary: World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.

papers.title: $QQ\bar Q\bar Q$ Quark System and Gauge/String Duality II: String Breaking
papers.summary: This is the second of two companion papers in which we continue developing the construction of the fully heavy tetraquark system using the gauge/string duality. Here, we extend this construction to model $SU(3)$ gauge theory with two light flavors of equal mass. As an application, we analyze the two lowest Born-Oppenheimer potentials, both analytically and numerically, for rectangular and collinear geometries. Our analysis reveals several critical scales associated with string reconnection and breaking, as well as junction annihilation and pinching. In addition, we find that the string tension is universal, whereas the string breaking distance is not.

papers.title: Do Language Models Mix? Experimental Evidence from Asymmetric Matching Pennies
papers.summary: I test whether language models can select and implement mixed strategies using asymmetric matching pennies and a task with prescribed choice probabilities. Several models respond to their own payoffs, contrary to equilibrium and resembling human experimental subjects. Without randomization tools, no tested model reliably implements prescribed probabilities. Prompting models with their choice histories alone does not resolve this failure. While an external randomizer sharply improves implementation, I find most models remain exploitable by an opportunistic opponent. These results provide guidance on the delegation of strategic decisions to AI systems based on language models.

papers.title: Exploratory Midtraining for Robot Policies
papers.summary: Robot policies predominantly learn from human-collected data emphasizing competent behavior, limiting coverage of the low-level behaviors needed to support autonomous improvement. We study how a form of midtraining can be used to build coverage over diverse low-level behaviors that connect challenging states of the robot and its environment to states from which further progress is possible ("connected behavioral coverage"). We also examine how this coverage supports downstream adaptation and online improvement. To this end, we introduce $β$-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation, where a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while a human operator continues toward completion without resetting. We relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. The resulting policy exhibits sustained use of more low-level behaviors. Across manipulation tasks in simulation and on three real-robot platforms, our approach yields more favorable data scaling laws, better zero-shot generalization, and more effective use of additional rollout time than training on standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, these policies need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates, suggesting that midtraining can prepare robots for both more robust task execution and continued autonomous improvement. Our project page and robot videos are available at https://kshitiz-1225.github.io/exploratory-midtraining-robot-policies/.

papers.title: Scalar perturbations in extremal Reissner-Nordström geometry: new methods at work
papers.summary: We study scalar radiation emitted by a particle moving along a circular orbit around a four-dimensional extremal Reissner-Nordström black hole. In particular, we calculate the energy fluxes carried by scalar waves to infinity and across the event horizon, as well as the scalar self-force acting on the particle, and express all these quantities as post-Newtonian expansions. Our results for the energy fluxes are in agreement with previous numerical findings in the literature. To solve the radial wave equation, we employ and test two distinct analytic approaches: the first is the so-called \textit{kink method}, a novel alternative stemming from quantum integrability and the second is the Mano-Suzuki-Takasugi method. The perfect agreement of the results highlights the potential of the kink method as a complementary tool for studying wave propagation in black-hole spacetimes.
papers.comment: Latex file and Mathematica ancillary file

papers.title: Neural Implicit Representation for Bathymetry Estimation using Sidescan Sonar Imagery
papers.summary: Bathymetry measurement and estimation is critical for understanding the structure of underwater environments. While multibeam echosounders (MBES) provide accurate depth measurements, their deployment on surface vessels limits spatial resolution in deep water. Sidescan sonar (SSS), in contrast, can be deployed on autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) to operate closer to the seafloor, enabling high-resolution acoustic imaging. However, the inherent ambiguity in measurements and the limited observation coverage of sonar datasets degrade the performance of state-of-the-art methods for underwater bathymetry estimation from SSS. In this paper, we propose a differentiable neural rendering framework for SSS that enables effective estimation of bathymetry from SSS measurements. Our approach incorporates a measurement model based on SSS geometry, explicitly accounting for its wide elevation aperture and associated ambiguities. We evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating improved robustness and accuracy compared to alternative approaches.
papers.comment: 7 pages, 8 figures. This paper is accepted by IEEE OCEANS 2026 Monterey

papers.title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
papers.summary: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess.
papers.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted manuscript of the paper published at the 2026 IEEE Gaming, Entertainment, and Media Conference (GEM). Code: https://github.com/Prof-it/temporal-chess-model; weights: https://huggingface.co/holymolyyy/temporal-chess-model
papers.journal: 2026 IEEE Gaming, Entertainment, and Media Conference (GEM), Berlin, Germany, 2026, pp. 1-6

papers.title: Evolutionary constraints on protein fold diversity
papers.summary: Arrangements of secondary structures in proteins yield a wide variety of possible topologies, yet the protein folds observed in nature are limited in their diversity. Is the number of protein folds limited by biophysical constraints or by evolutionary contingency? In recent years, the development of new methods for protein structure prediction and comparison, molecular design, and the rapid progress of cryo-electron microscopy revealed new insights into the protein fold space. Here, we present recent findings demonstrating that natural proteins adopt only a small fraction of all possible folds and discuss how evolutionary processes limit the diversity of evolving protein folds.

papers.title: From dispersal to patrol: the extracellular matrix shapes an annealing-like search by Drosophila embryonic macrophages
papers.summary: Hemocytes, the macrophages of Drosophila, disperse through the embryo and then patrol its tissues, moving along basement membranes that they help to build.
